Catalog Description

Modern and Contemporary Drama. (3-0). Credit 3. Representative plays and performances from the late nineteenth century to the present. Prerequisite: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

Additional Course Details

Immersive storytelling is associated today primarily with contemporary media—especially computer games, fantasy novels, RPGs, escape rooms and virtual reality experiences—but the original artistic genre that was devised to maximize immediacy and impact is drama. At once social and intimate, simultaneously literary and corporeal, the theatre has historically been an important scene (pun intended) of public art. Unique among artistic genres, drama can be understood as a dynamic interface collectively produced by writers, professionals, performances, and audiences. As such, it offers students of literature a special view into the power of words. Although we will acknowledge (and experience) the fundamental position of performance, which now is enabled through an exciting variety of avenues, from the traditional to the digital and from multi-level, multi-million-dollar venues to black box theatres and off-off-off Broadway nooks, our class is in an English department rather than a theatre, performance or drama department. Consequently, our literary-critical approach will focus on close-reading texts to understand plays as highly charged and influential reactions to cultural conditions. As we read our plays, we will view filmed or live performances to give more dimension to our textually based class.

Unit 1, Modern Marriage, will cover from the late-nineteenth century to WWII. To lend cohesion to this historical range yet remain true to the turbulent emergence and ebbing of new dramatic genres, we will read three different accounts of marriage. First, Henrik Ibsen’s Hedda Gabler will exemplify the “problem play” genre of modernist art, introduce us to one of drama’s most iconic heroines, and emphasize the transnational nature of Anglophone theatre. To leaven Ibsen’s piercing seriousness, we’ll turn to Oscar Wilde’s The Importance of Being Earnest and recover the social and artistic implications of his satirical exaggeration of the “well-made play.” Lastly, we’ll discuss the avant-garde explosion of the well-made model with Sophie Treadwell’s Machinal, which defied these earlier conventions to reveal aspects of marriage that go unremarked by Ibsen and Wilde.

Unit 2, Revisionist Histories, will push further into the 20th century and focus on plays that emphatically serve as interventions in popular understandings of history. Our first play interrogates the underpinnings of modern nation-states: Arthur Miller’s The Crucible (which soberly depicts the Salem Witch Trials as an allegory for McCarthyism). By rewriting history in dramatic form, Miller shows how much of politics—all the way from international affairs and national governance to family dynamics and interpersonal affairs—rests on the creation of persuasive spectacles. As we learn more about the details of the real-life people and events staged by Miller, we’ll discuss the interdependency of politics and theatre. By way of August Wilson’s Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom, which looks backward from the 1980s to the recording of a jazz album in the 1920s, we’ll finish the unit by uncovering how these historical reevaluations can tell us about the real-life conditions of artistic production. We will end this unit with a play of local and regional significance: Lucy Prebble’s ENRON, a courtroom drama of the fall of its eponymous Texas corporation.

Throughout the semester, you are responsible for keeping up with the readings listed above, attending class, and taking part of discussions and live readings of scenes from the plays. You’ll also take daily quizzes on the reading for that day; complete one creative writing assignment to demonstrate your understanding of playwrights’ diverse styles; participate in a group project that proposes a new adaptation of a play on our syllabus; and write a critical review essay of a live or taped theatrical performance.

Course Prerequisites

Prerequisite/Corequisite(s): 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

Course Learning Outcomes

Upon completion of this course, the learner will be able to:

  • Recall key events, themes, and characters in plays representative of modern drama
  • Identify, describe, and emulate the writing style of individual dramatists
  • Recognize references to cultural, economic, and political histories in artworks and understand the artists’ commentaries upon those histories
  • Hypothesize the likely impact of individual plays upon the audiences that viewed the performances
  • Compare and contrast aspects of plot, character, scenery, dialogue, direction, etc, within the text versus their materializations in particular performances
  • Engage with local and campus-based opportunities for theatrical immersion and spectatorship

Special Course Designation

KICD - University Required International & Cultural Diversity

Objectives for International and Cultural Diversity (ICD):

  • Live and work effectively in a diverse and global society: This course will teach students how to incorporate historical contexts on global issues to analyze literature; how to work in small groups, incorporating differing viewpoints to produce a collective response to an issue; and, in the final weeks of the class, how one play understands Texas's position in global energy systems as a context for the analysis of regional cultural production. Their final review paper will require them to articulate the way that an existing play adaptation models living and working in a global society and evaluate the effectiveness of the characters' strategies for doing so.

  • Articulate the value of a diverse and global perspective: This course provides the opportunity for students to read/view and reflect on texts from a variety of cultural perspectives as well introducing them to lecture material that includes further cultural viewpoints and global/ transnational perspectives, especially by showing how various cultures have received (reacted to) course texts. Their group project will require them to acknowledge these perspectives and use them to shape an adaptation proposal.

  • Recognize diverse opinions and practices (including but not limited to economic, political, gender, and religious opinions) and consider different points of view: This course will offer a number of opportunities for students to engage with, reflect on, and research, both in writing and in discussion, viewpoints that are different from their own. A creative writing assignment asks students to consider their own life events from other viewpoints.

Grading Policy

Grade Breakdown

Attendance: 10%

Reading Quizzes: 35%

Rewrite Your Life: 20%

Propose an Adaptation: 20%

Review a Performance: 15%


Attendance: I will take roll at the beginning of each class session. For each day, arriving on time and staying the whole class yields 100%. Arriving late or leaving early will receive 80%. 0% is given for an unexcused absence. An excused absence will be entirely left out of your attendance calculations.


Reading Quizzes: A five-question multiple choice reading quiz taken in the first 10 minutes of class will test whether you understood the main events and characters in that day's reading. The quiz will not attempt to trap students with minutiae or entangle them in complex abstractions, but merely ensure that the reading has been completed and understood at a basic level of accuracy before class discussion begins.


Rewrite Your Life: You will pick some scene from your own life and write it in two different styles that you have encountered thus far in class. This event, moment, or conversation from your life can be entirely normal (no need for high drama or confession!) The point is to shape a moment in your life into an exchange of dialogue, together with some stage directions and scenery description. Choosing two out of the three options below, write two 3-4 page scenes in the following styles:

  • a realist style, trying to be as accurate, natural, and serious as possible (Ibsen).
  • a highly comedic style, exaggerating what you wrote before to highlight its absurdity, heighten its wit, and skewer its underlying assumptions (Wilde)
  • a tense, expressionistic style, turning inward to reveal the inner emotions of the characters and, possibly, consider any horror undertones in the scene or highlight the role of the machines your characters may be interacting with (Treadwell).

Propose an Adaptation: In groups of 3-4, you will choose a play, assess the current range of its adaptations and performances, and then propose a new one that will address the needs of a different, contemporary audience and/or take advantage of new media of entertainment or technologies of representation. You will fill out a comprehensive worksheet that will guide you through this process, then create some sample or prototype (such as a 5-10-minute performance, 3-minute trailer, an annotated cast + crew list, a detailed yet consistent mood board, a storyboard for a substantial scene, sample script pages, or an elevator pitch). Groups of two or five will be accepted, but the standards for the final product will be lowered for two people and raised for five. You will also participate in a presentation to the entire class (with a demonstration of your prototype) and fill out a questionnaire about your precise roles/duties within your group.


Review a Performance: You will attend a live performance of any play of your choice, or you will view a taped TV/film recording that is specifically a performance of a play that is included on our syllabus. You will write a 4-5-page, double-spaced review that reflects knowledge of the performance (what organization is behind it? what theatre? which actors, directors, etc?), theorizes the intentions or purpose of the production (why are they doing it? why now? what do they hope to achieve?), and assesses whether the quality of the adaptation makes it a productive, beautiful, stimulating, or relevant work of art.


Grading Scale

This class follows the College of Arts & Sciences Grading Scale, which runs as follows:

A = 90-100

B = 80-89

C = 70-79

D = 60-69

F = 0-59

You will turn this in according to University policy (e.g., generally within two weeks of the relevant excused absence.)

AI Statement

The only acceptable AI use in this class will be in a particular, limited way for the Adapt a Proposal group project. Groups may use AI to create visual, video, or audio samples of the proposed adaptation or promotional materials for the proposed adaptation (such as posters and slides). Groups are certainly not required to use AI for successful project. No group may use AI for brainstorming purposes (e.g., your ideas about how to propose the play need to be from each other, not an AI-generated idea). Also, no group may use AI to answer the questions on the worksheet that you must produce. Finally, no group may use AI to deliver the in-class presentation (that is, you must actually present to the class live in person!)


Throughout the entire course, AI may not be used a substitute for 1) doing the reading oneself, 2) brainstorming ideas for your major assignments, 3) producing those essay assignments (even if you later edit them yourself), or 4) completing quizzes.


Suspected AI use under these categories, or suspected AI use for the group project that does not fall under the allowed usage stipulated above, will be documented and submitted to the Honor Council for arbitration as outlined by University policy.

University Policies

This section outlines the university-level policies that must be included in each course syllabus. The TAMU Faculty Advisory Council established the wording of these policies.

Academic Integrity Statement and Policy

“An Aggie does not lie, cheat or steal, or tolerate those who do.”

“Texas A&M University students are responsible for authenticating all work submitted to an instructor. If asked, students must be able to produce proof that the item submitted is indeed the work of that student. Students must keep appropriate records at all times. The inability to authenticate one’s work, should the instructor request it, may be sufficient grounds to initiate an academic misconduct case” (Section 20.1.2.3, Student Rule 20).

You can learn more about the Aggie Honor System Office Rules and Procedures, academic integrity, and your rights and responsibilities at aggiehonor.tamu.edu.

University Attendance Policy

The university views class attendance and participation as an individual student responsibility. Students are expected to attend class and to complete all assignments.

Please refer to Student Rule 7 in its entirety for information about excused absences, including definitions, and related documentation and timelines.

Course Specific Attendance Policy

If you suffer an illness or experience an emergency that makes it impossible to attend, you must provide timely documentation to make this absence excused. Consult A&M Student Rule #7 for an explanation about what can be excused and what isn’t admissible as an excuse. For any absence, whether excused or unexcused, you need to check Canvas for any course announcements you may have missed and review the PowerPoint I put on Canvas for that day. If anything is unclear after reviewing the slideshow and checking the announcements page, then ask other students, email me, or attend office hours.

Makeup Work Policy

Students will be excused from attending class on the day of a graded activity or when attendance contributes to a student’s grade, for the reasons stated in Student Rule 7, or other reason deemed appropriate by the instructor.

Please refer to Student Rule 7 in its entirety for information about makeup work, including definitions, and related documentation and timelines.

Absences related to Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 may necessitate a period of more than 30 days for make-up work, and the timeframe for make-up work should be agreed upon by the student and instructor” (Student Rule 7, Section 7.4.1).

“The instructor is under no obligation to provide an opportunity for the student to make up work missed because of an unexcused absence” (Student Rule 7, Section 7.4.2).

Students who request an excused absence are expected to uphold the Aggie Honor Code and Student Conduct Code. (See Student Rule 24.)

Notice of Nondiscrimination

The University provides equal opportunity to all employees, students, applicants for employment or admission, and the public, regardless of race, color, sex (including pregnancy and related conditions), religion, national origin, age, disability, genetic information, or veteran status.

Texas A&M University will promptly, thoroughly, and fairly investigate and resolve all complaints of discrimination, harassment (including sexual harassment), complicity, and related retaliation based on a protected class in accordance with System Regulation 08.01.01, University Rule 08.01.01.M1, Standard Administrative Procedure (SAP) 08.01.01.M1.01, and applicable federal and state laws. In accordance with Title IX and its implementing regulations, Texas A&M does not discriminate on the basis of sex in any educational program or activity, including admissions and employment.

The following person has been designated to handle inquiries and complaints regarding the non-discrimination policies: Jennifer M. Smith, TAMU Associate VP & Title IX Coordinator at YMCA Ste 108, College Station, TX 77843, 979-458-8407, or email civilrights@tamu.edu. For other reporting options, visit the U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights Complaint Assessment System to locate the address and phone number of the office that serves your area, or call 1-800-421-3481.

Civil Rights, Free Speech, and Title IX Policies

Texas A&M University is committed to fostering a learning environment that is safe and productive for all. University policies and federal and state laws prohibit discrimination and harassment based on an individual’s race, color, sex, (including pregnancy and related conditions), religion, national origin, age, disability, genetic information, veteran status, or any other legally protected characteristic. This includes forms of sex-based violence, such as sexual assault, sexual harassment, sexual exploitation, dating/domestic violence, and stalking.

Students can report discrimination/harassment, access supportive resources, or learn more about their options for resolving complaints on the University’s Civil Rights & Title IX webpage.

Students should be aware that all university employees (except medical or mental health providers) are mandatory reporters, which means that if they observe, experience or become aware of an incident that they reasonably believe to be discrimination/harassment alleged to have been committed by or against a person who was a student or employee at the time of the incident, the employee must report the incident to the university.

Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Policy

Texas A&M University is committed to providing equitable access to learning opportunities for all students. If you experience barriers to your education due to a disability or think you may have a disability, please contact the Disability Resources office on your campus (resources listed below). Disabilities may include, but are not limited to, attentional, learning, mental health, sensory, physical, or chronic health conditions. All students are encouraged to discuss their disability-related needs with Disability Resources and their instructors as soon as possible.

To request academic accommodations, contact the designated ADA office based on your location:

  • Texas A&M University, College of Nursing, College of Dentistry, Irma Lerma Rangel College of Pharmacy College Station, College of Medicine, School of Public Health, Institute of Biosciences and Technology, EnMed Program, Bush School in Washington DC, Mays Business School – CityCentre, TAMU Engineering Academies, Texas A&M University Higher Education Center at McAllen and Texas A&M University at Galveston should contact Disability Resources at (979) 845-1637 or disability@tamu.edu.
  • Texas A&M University School of Law should contact the Office of Student Affairs at (817) 212-4111 or law-disability@law.tamu.edu to request accommodations.
  • Irma Lerma Rangel College of Pharmacy in Kingsville should contact the Disability Resource Center at Texas A&M University-Kingsville at (361) 593-3024 or drc.center@tamuk.edu to request accommodations.
  • Texas A&M University College of Veterinary Medicine & Biomedical Sciences in Canyon should contact the Office of Student Accessibility at West Texas A&M University – Canyon at (806) 651-2335 or osa@wtamu.edu.

If you are experiencing difficulties with your approved accommodations, contact the office responsible for approving your accommodations or the Texas A&M ADA Coordinator Julie Kuder at ADA.Coordinator@tamu.edu or (979) 458-8407.

Pregnancy Accommodations

Texas A&M provides reasonable accommodations to students due to pregnancy and/or related conditions, such as childbirth, recovery, and lactation. Students should contact the University’s Pregnancy Coordinator as soon as they become aware of the need for accommodation. Depending on the circumstances, accommodations could include extended time to complete assignments or exams, changes in course sequence, or modifications to the physical classroom environment.

Texas A&M will also allow a voluntary leave of absence, ensure the availability of lactation space, and maintain grievance procedures to provide for the prompt and equitable resolution of complaints of sex discrimination. For information regarding pregnancy accommodations, email TIX.Pregnancy@tamu.edu.

Statement on Mental Health and Wellness

Texas A&M University recognizes that mental health and wellness are critical factors influencing a student’s academic success and overall wellbeing. Students are encouraged to engage in healthy self-care practices by utilizing the resources and services available through University Health Services. The TELUS Health Student Support app provides access to professional counseling in multiple languages anytime, anywhere by phone or chat, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline offers 24-hour emergency support at 988 or 988lifeline.org.

Texas A&M College Station

Students needing a listening ear can contact University Health Services at 979.458.4584. Call 911 or visit your nearest emergency room if you are currently experiencing a life-threatening situation or if your safety is at risk. 24-hour emergency help is also available through the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (988) or at 988lifeline.org.

Statement on the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)

FERPA is a federal law designed to protect the privacy of educational records by limiting access to these records, to establish the right of students to inspect and review their educational records, and to provide guidelines for the correction of inaccurate and misleading data through informal and formal hearings.

Currently enrolled students wishing to withhold any or all directory information items can do so within howdy.tamu.edu using the Directory Information Withholding Form. The complete FERPA Notice to Students and the student records policy is available on the Office of the Registrar webpage.

Items that can never be identified as public information are a student’s social security number, citizenship, gender, grades, GPR, or class schedule. All efforts will be made in this class to protect your privacy and to ensure confidential treatment of information associated with or generated by your participation in the class.

Directory items include name, UIN, local address, permanent address, email address, local telephone number, permanent telephone number, dates of attendance, program of study (college, major, campus), classification, previous institutions attended, degrees, honors and awards received, participation in officially recognized activities and sports, medical residence location, and medical residence specialization.

Free Speech and Civil Discourse

Texas A&M recognizes that the pursuit of truth through open and robust discourse is critical to academic inquiry. However, as a community of scholars, the university has an aspirational expectation that such discourse will be conducted in accordance with Aggie Core Values. In this “marketplace of ideas,” we encourage civil dialogue creating an environment that allows individuals to express their ideas and to have their ideas challenged in respectful and responsible ways. Students can learn more about Freedom of Expression and Free Speech on the University's website about the First Amendment.
